title: The second arrow
hookLine: pain is one arrow; the distress we add is a second (SN 36.6)

cards: You stub your toe on the bed frame at night. There's the pain, sharp and real. And then, within a second: who put this bed here, why am I so clumsy, this always happens to me, now I'll never get back to sleep.
The toe hurt for thirty seconds. The rest of it went on for twenty minutes. The Buddha gave a short teaching about exactly this, with a picture from the battlefield.

teach.b: It's in the Connected Discourses, a sutta called the Arrow. The Buddha asks his monks: when an ordinary person and a well-trained disciple both feel pain, what's the difference? Then he answers with an image.
An untrained person, touched by a painful feeling, worries, grieves, laments, beats their chest and becomes distraught.

teach.h: STRUCK BY ONE, THEN BY A SECOND.
teach.b: It's as if they were struck by an arrow, and then by a second arrow right after. They feel two pains: one in the body, one in the mind.
The well-trained disciple, touched by the same painful feeling, doesn't add the worry and the lament. They are struck by one arrow, not a second: they feel the bodily pain, and not the other.
Notice what the Buddha doesn't say. He doesn't say the trained person feels no pain.

teach.h: THE FIRST ARROW LANDS ON EVERYONE.
teach.b: The first arrow lands on everyone, including, other texts say, the Buddha himself, who had back pain and grew old.

teach.h: THE SECOND IS THE ONE WE FIRE.
teach.b: The teaching is only about the second arrow, the one a person fires at themselves. And he adds something sharp.

When pain comes, the untrained person often runs toward sensual pleasure to escape it, because they know no other way out. That's a third trap, hidden inside the second. It links straight back to yesterday.
The second arrow is what comes next. See the feeling as just a feeling, and the second arrow never leaves the bow.

how: Buddhist teachers of many schools use the two arrows image from the Sallatha Sutta, and versions of it appear in some pain-care and mindfulness courses to separate physical pain from the distress added to it.

o: a bow, the Buddha's image for discipline
a shield that blocks every kind of pain
an arrow, the Buddha's image for pain

games.q: match each piece of the arrow teaching.
p: worry, grief and lament we add
the trap hidden in the second

s: the teaching says a trained person feels no pain
the first arrow lands on everyone; the teaching is about the second.
the Buddha himself is said to have had physical pain
the texts mention his backaches and old age.
the second arrow is the distress we add on top
worry, grieving, lamenting: a second pain in the mind.

games.q: you're one of the Buddha's monks, and he asks: when an ordinary person and a trained disciple both feel pain, what's the difference?
o: the trained disciple feels no pain at all.
the trained disciple feels the body's pain but doesn't add a second pain of distress.
games.why: both are struck by the first arrow. only the untrained person is struck by the second.

practice: Find some small discomfort, a stiff knee, an itch, a tight shoulder or a worry you've been carrying, and feel the first arrow: just the raw sensation, or the plain fact.
Then watch for the second arrow, the story, the complaint, the why me, and when it comes, name it quietly: second arrow. Return to the first, and let it be only what it is.

wordCard.voice: Salla. The Pali word for an arrow: the first one is the pain itself, which lands on everyone; the second, which we fire ourselves, is the one to watch for.

orig.note: Pali salla: an arrow or dart; the sutta's name is Sallatha, the arrow.

carryVoice: Your line: one arrow, not two. The first lands on everyone; the second is the one to watch. That's day two hundred fifty-seven.
